source.title: Minimum $\ell_{1}$-norm interpolators: Precise asymptotics and multiple descent

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes risk as model dimension varies and reports multiple-descent results, but uses theoretical and numerical methods for sparse linear regression rather than the original deep-network settings.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own risk characterization and simulations. Background descriptions of double descent and results cited from other work are not recorded as findings. The study does not vary training epochs or sample size at fixed model dimension.
record.test_reason: The study derives exact asymptotic risk, with simulations, for the minimum ℓ1-norm interpolator in sparse linear regression as p/n varies. This is a new model class beyond deep networks, and it yields a model-capacity risk curve with a peak at p=n, renewed descent past interpolation, and an additional ascent-descent phase (triple or multiple descent). These results bear directly on V4 and on the multiple-peak part of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors prove, via an exact two-equation risk characterization from AMP, that the minimum ℓ1 interpolator's risk can descend and ascend multiple times as p/n grows. This is triple descent when sparsity is small, caused by ℓ1 geometry and its interplay with sparsity, unlike the double descent of the minimum ℓ2 interpolator. Two points should be added: at very large p/n the risk tends to that of the zero estimator, and at larger sparsity the over-parameterized descent may be monotone (stated as a possibility, not proven).
record.recipe_differences: The study derives risk behavior for minimum `1-norm interpolation in sparse linear regression using asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations, rather than testing deep networks or their training procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk-curve behavior changes with the sparsity ratio; the paper reports multiple descent at sufficiently low sparsity and possible monotone descent over the over-parameterized range at higher sparsity.
record.problems: The central theoretical results assume i.i.d. Gaussian design and proportional high-dimensional asymptotics. The finite-sample and non-Gaussian evidence is numerical; simulations use 30 trials, and the text does not provide numerical error-bar sizes.
record.rows_left_out: The theoretical minimum `2-norm comparison in Figure 3 is not separately rowed because it is a comparator rather than the study's minimum `1-norm result. Figure 7 concerns coordinate distributions, not the risk-curve versions.

untested.parts: No deep networks; only linear minimum ℓ1 interpolation.
No training-time axis. The 'epoch-based' AMP is a proof device, not a risk-over-training measurement.
Sample size is not varied at fixed p.
Only the minimum ℓ1 interpolator under i.i.d. (mainly Gaussian) design. Correlated designs are explicitly left open.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peaks (noise level not varied; SNR held fixed), and whether optimally tuned regularization removes them (only the λ→0 Lasso limit is studied).
No recounting of complexity by effective parameters.

missing.what: Theoretical risk curves for ε=0.5, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 at SNR=2. An extra descent phase appears only when ε drops below a level; the minimum ℓ2 curve shows a single over-parameterized descent. This is the main evidence that multiple descent depends on sparsity.
Risk blows up as p/n→1 (τ* diverges as δ→1; OLS risk δσ²/(δ−1) for p<n), i.e. the peak sits at the interpolation threshold.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source, so verdicts apply. The tranche was changed from the reader's T2 to T3, because this is a new model class giving a result on the general curve (V4). Theorem 1(a)–(c) together imply risk rises above Risk(0) and then descends back to it at large p/n. Noise level is never varied (σ normalized to 1, SNR fixed), so the noise-driven part of V6 is untested rather than challenged.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks and the model-wise curve in the claim's original deep-network settings.
Increasing sample size near the interpolation threshold at fixed model dimension.
The study tests model-capacity risk curves for minimum-norm linear regression, not all model classes.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across axes.
Whether varying label noise or variance causes the peaks, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
Recounting complexity by an effective number of parameters.

rows.value: Risk increases with p/n in a region between the two ranges of descent; the authors describe the resulting pattern as potentially triple descent when combined with under-parameterized behavior.
rows.note: This is evidence of an additional ascent and descent phase. The result is conditional on sparsity and does not establish a noise-driven cause.
rows.check: Observed as an extra ascent-descent (multiple descent) for V6. For V4 the same row is a qualification: risk rises again inside the over-parameterized regime, so improvement past interpolation is not monotone.

source_check.correct: V4: reversed within the identified increasing-risk interval. V6: observed for the multiple-descent component.
source_check.problem: A single observed state obscures that this interval reverses V4's improvement while contributing to V6's multiple descent.

rows.subject: minimum `1-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Theorem gives the limiting risk as p/n tends to infinity.
rows.value: Risk approaches the risk of the zero estimator.
rows.note: The authors also state that the risk decreases in the large-ratio region.
rows.check: The late descent converges to Risk(0), the zero estimator's risk. Section 3.2's proof of 1(c) shows risk can dip below Risk(0) and then rise back. So the second descent ends at trivial-estimator performance, not continued improvement; the row's note should say so.

source_check.correct: V4: cannot_determine from this limiting-value result alone; decreasing risk at large p/n is established separately by Theorem 1(a).
source_check.problem: Convergence to the zero estimator's risk alone does not establish a descending capacity-wise curve.

tranche.reason: Sparse minimum ℓ1 interpolation supplies a new estimator setting with theoretical and simulated results on capacity-wise double and multiple descent.

source_check.notes: The study does not test noise-driven peak splitting or peak elimination under optimally tuned regularization. The eventual descent approaches Risk(0); the below-Risk(0) dip and subsequent ascent occur before that final descending regime.

statements.correction: At SNR=2, sufficiently small sparsity produces an extra descent for minimum ℓ1 interpolation; minimum ℓ2 interpolation has one descending phase for p>n. Noise causation and elimination under optimal regularization are not tested.
statements.problem: The sparsity and estimator comparisons are accurate, but they do not establish a limitation of V6's existential multiple-descent component or exclude noise/variance explanations.
